thread_title: S. flava var. cuprea (ex. Bill Hoyer)
breadcrumb: S. flava var. cuprea (ex. Bill Hoyer)

posts.body_html:
If you read the description of S. flava var. cuprea and you want to stick by the book, then you can say this Bill Hoyer clone isn't S. flava var. cuprea. However, be careful with believing the current naming scheme, as it doesn't account for phenotypic variation in cultivation. Growing this clone under various environmental conditions shows you can bring out phenotypes that are otherwise not noticed in both the wild and under normal growing conditions. All of the darkest, most prominent coppery topped "cupreas" I've ever grown at some point produced reddish bodies, and for the sake of simplicity, I consider them all to be genuine cupreas.

Some claim that if the body of a S. flava does color up, then it's an atropurpurea, even if it looks like a cuprea under most normal growing conditions. After growing out many cuprea clones, I'm starting to find that very few cuprea clones DO NOT color up slightly on the body of the trap under certain environmental conditions.

In the case of S. flava var. cuprea 'Bill Hoyer,' the reddish coloration might be due to excessive direct sunlight and very cold days/nights. For the past several years, this clone has never produced a reddish body to the extent that it is now, but we haven't had cold spring weather like this in many years. Under normal years, the reddish pigments do show up just a little bit on the body, perhaps not noticeably enough to get people's attention. This year is different.

Just as an aside, Sarracenia flava var. atropurpurea 'Waccamaw' was selfed, and one of the offspring was a cuprea! Anyhow, here's S. flava var. cuprea 'Bill Hoyer' Photos taken 4/2/18:


I have verified atropurpurea clones right now that have greener traps than this LOL

Yes, on the copper coloured upper pitcher and hood plants. I think S. flava Copper Top is the most fitting name for that colour presentation of flava. But I won't go down the variety naming road again.

The Copper Top from Waccamaw is no surprise (but a welcome one, of course). Highlights the Carolina lineage of the thing and the familial relationship between the two distinctive colour types of flava found in that region.

Some new pics of Bill Hoyer, the plant, not the homie! I think the last time I saw Bill Hoyer aka "Little Billy Hoyer" (as Peter D'Amato likes to call him) was when I was 16 years old! Peter met us older heads when we were teens, so he still remembers us as such even though we're old ass men now LOL Anyways, Bill is actually a really academically intelligent dude who last I heard was doing some nerdy hardcore science stuff on one of the islands off of California.

but anyways, the legacy of his plant that he bought from California Carnivores as a kid and then had to give back goes on! S. flava var. cuprea 'Bill Hoyer' photos taken 4/23/19, and this is a recent division guys:

posts.body_html: I remember Damon of California Carnivores saying years ago that he thought this is the best cuprea clone in cultivation due to its ease of coloring up, vigor, and the potential size they can reach. I have a bigger mother plant crowded in a community tray that's sizing up, maybe next year they'll be gigantic, we'll see! For now, check out these recent divisions, they still colored up all the way! Pics taken mostly on 5/16/22:

posts.body_html:
Had a trap that was knocked down by the wind due to its height, so I harvested it to show you that these traps are tall AF!
Some of you see lots of red pigments and are wondering what does tall Anthocyanin Free mean? Others are likely nodding their heads, think yes, Mr. Dubz, that's pretty tall, guys.

Pics taken 5/20/25:



the top of the lid on that tall thang:


collection the background, so you know this ain't no imposter Mike Wang




So hard to tell the size of this mother plant, but with the trap above, I think you can get an idea now. Most traps are equally tall:


Even the divisions are quite impressive:
